learningObjective: Convert a broad claim that a technique is overrated into a defensible judgment by naming the targeted use, failure mechanism, useful boundary, and evidence that could update the position.
mediumRationale: A two-panel semantic HTML comparison is the smallest medium that can align an unsupported verdict with the four missing parts of a bounded critique. It keeps the reader focused on the structure of technical judgment rather than implying that the example techniques have a universal ranking.

mediumComparison.mermaid: Rejected because the lesson is a matched comparison, not a process with directional flow; arrows would falsely imply that every opinion is formed in one fixed sequence.
mediumComparison.svg: Rejected because there is no quantitative geometry to draw, and SVG text would be less adaptable than native table semantics at 390 CSS pixels.
mediumComparison.semanticHtml: Selected because two labelled panels and native row headers expose the exact correspondence between a vague claim and a bounded critique, remain readable without JavaScript, and stack using established responsive primitives.
mediumComparison.interaction: Rejected because toggling techniques or scoring an opinion would add state and imply a universal rubric; the evidence and boundary must remain use-case-specific.
mediumComparison.paperReuse: Rejected because the papers contain task-specific experiments rather than a general interview-answer structure. Public access is not treated as artwork permission, and no figure, data, wording, or layout is copied.
mediumComparison.noVisual: Rejected because the prose lists strong-answer qualities but leaves readers to mentally align them with a concrete claim. The matched rows make the missing scope, mechanism, boundary, and evidence immediately diagnosable.

pages.insight: The model-selection slide contrasts real data, augmentation, synthetic data, pretraining, dropout, weight decay, early stopping, and model size with explicit situational caveats; it demonstrates bounded recommendations but provides no interview-answer framework.

The neighboring training-practice slide recommends distilling an ensemble when test-time computation is unaffordable, presenting distillation as a deployment tradeoff rather than a universal quality gain.
The following slide begins basic probabilistic ML algorithms and adds no evidence-boundary or interview guidance.
The preceding transformer overview describes architecture families, scaling costs, and training stability but does not discuss chain-of-thought prompting.
The chain-of-thought slide proposes code training as an intuition for emergent step-by-step reasoning while explicitly noting that hard evidence is absent and the source remains open.
The following LLM slide discusses model families and Toolformer, including a bounded calculator-like benefit from tool use, but no generic prompting rule.
The preceding section divider introduces model compression and contains no technical comparison.
The compression slide defines distillation as a student mimicking teacher outputs or representations and discusses architecture-dependent transfer, alongside pruning and quantization tradeoffs.
The following slide changes to recommender systems and adds no distillation boundary.
The preceding slide covers binary representation and coding questions, not opinion formation or behavioral interviewing.
The deck's behavioral and culture interview page is only a section divider, so it supplies no model answer, evaluation rubric, or visual to reuse.
The following resources page links to behavioral and general interview material but contains no substantive guidance for defending a technical opinion.

deckReview.notes: The complete 214-page deck was text-indexed page by page for overrated, opinion, behavioral or culture, chain of thought, distillation, and synthetic data. Exact matches led to full review of pages 62-64, 103-105, 127-129, and 206-208. The deck contains technique-specific fragments and only a behavioral section divider; it never combines a scoped target, causal mechanism, useful boundary, and updating evidence. No slide artwork, wording, data, or layout is reused.

sources.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
sources.usage: Used as the primary source showing that chain-of-thought prompting was evaluated on specified arithmetic, symbolic, and commonsense benchmarks across model scales, supporting a task- and model-bounded claim rather than a generic quality guarantee.
sources.license: The arXiv record is freely viewable, but a permissive license for adapting its figures was not established. No prompt example, result, data, prose, figure, or layout is copied.

sources.title: Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network
sources.usage: Used as the primary source for distillation's deployment framing: transfer a cumbersome model's learned mapping and soft targets into a smaller model subject to deployment requirements, with the paper noting that the student typically cannot exactly match those targets.
sources.license: The paper is publicly accessible, but public access is not treated as figure-reuse permission. The visual reproduces no soft-target example, equation, experiment, wording, or artwork.

sources.title: The Curse of Recursion: Training on Generated Data Makes Models Forget
sources.usage: Used as primary evidence that generated-data risks depend on a concrete training regime: recursive replacement and approximation or sampling errors can compound, rather than synthetic data being uniformly beneficial or harmful.
sources.license: No permissive figure-reuse grant was established from the arXiv landing page. No source distribution, equation, result, dataset, prose, figure, or composition is reused.

sources.title: arXiv License Information
sources.usage: Used as the official licensing reference to verify that arXiv hosts works under multiple licenses and that free viewing alone does not establish adaptation rights.
sources.license: The policy is cited only to document licensing treatment. No policy text, icon, or page design is reproduced.

sourceReview.notes: The complete article's hardest prose-only mental model is the difference between contrarian preference and evidence-bounded technical judgment. The figure is an original article-specific comparison, not a synthesis of any source figure. Its CoT row is explicitly an example critique to test in a use case, not a universal empirical law: target, mechanism, boundary, and metric must all be defended. The cited primary papers cross-check why the candidate techniques require scoped claims, while the original visual teaches the reusable answer structure.

agentReview.summary: Read the complete article, text-indexed all 214 deck pages and inspected four exact slide neighborhoods, then reviewed primary work on chain-of-thought prompting, knowledge distillation, and recursive generated-data training plus official arXiv licensing guidance before selecting an original matched semantic comparison.

implementation.accessibility: The figure uses native headings, sections, tables, row headers, and explicit accessible labels. Missing questions and completed answers carry the comparison without color; the highlighted target cell is supplementary. The established two-panel grid stacks below 640 pixels, and short native text wraps at 390 CSS pixels without horizontal scrolling. Existing theme variables provide dark-mode contrast, established print rules force a light high-contrast palette and avoid splitting the figure, and the lesson remains available with CSS or JavaScript disabled.
